content: In this chapter, we study two representations of graphs and basic algorithms that use these representations. Mathematically, a \emph{(directed) graph} \index{graph} \index{directed graph} is a pair $G=(V,E)$ where $V$ is a set of \emph{vertices} \index{vertex} and $E$ is a set of ordered pairs of vertices called \emph{edges}. \index{edge} An edge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{j}})}} is \emph{directed} \index{directed edge} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}; \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is called the \emph{source} \index{source} of the edge and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} is called the \emph{target}. \index{target} A \emph{path} \index{path} in $G$ is a sequence of vertices $v_0,\ldots,v_k$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$, the edge $(v_{i-1},v_{i})$ is in $E$. A path $v_0,\ldots,v_k$ is a \emph{cycle} \index{cycle} if, additionally, the edge $(v_k,v_0)$ is in $E$. A path (or cycle) is \emph{simple} \index{simple path/cycle} if all of its vertices are unique. If there is a path from some vertex $v_i$ to some vertex $v_j$ then we say that $v_j$ is \emph{reachable} \index{reachable vertex} from $v_i$. An example of a graph is shown in \figref{graph}.

Due to their ability to model so many phenomena, graphs have an enormous number of applications. There are many obvious examples. Computer networks can be modelled as graphs, with vertices corresponding to computers and edges corresponding to (directed) communication links between those computers. City streets can be modelled as graphs, with vertices representing intersections and edges representing streets joining consecutive intersections. Less obvious examples occur as soon as we realize that graphs can model any pairwise relationships within a set. content: \seclabel{adjacency-list} \index{adjacency list} \emph{Adjacency list} representations of graphs take a more vertex-centric approach. There are many possible implementations of adjacency lists. In this section, we present a simple one. At the end of the section, we discuss different possibilities. In an adjacency list representation, the graph $G=(V,E)$ is represented as an array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{adj}}}}, of lists. The list \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{adj}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}} contains a list of all the vertices adjacent to vertex \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. That is, it contains every index \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} such that $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{j}})}}\in E$.

content: Breadth-First Search
raw_latex: \subsection{Breadth-First Search}

content: \index{breadth-first-search} The \emph{breadth-first-search} algorithm starts at a vertex \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} and visits, first the neighbours of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, then the neighbours of the neighbours of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, then the neighbours of the neighbours of the neighbours of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, and so on. This algorithm is a generalization of the breadth-first traversal algorithm for binary trees (\secref{bintree:traversal}), and is very similar; it uses a queue, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}, that initially contains only \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}. It then repeatedly extracts an element from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} and adds its neighbours to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}, provided that these neighbours have never been in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} before. The only major difference between the breadth-first-search algorithm for graphs and the one for trees is that the algorithm for graphs has to ensure that it does not add the same vertex to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} more than once. It does this by using an auxiliary boolean array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{seen}}}}, that tracks which vertices have already been discovered.

A breadth-first traversal has some very special properties. Calling \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} will eventually enqueue (and eventually dequeue) every vertex \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} such that there is a directed path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}. Moreover, the vertices at distance 0 from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} itself) will enter \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} before the vertices at distance 1, which will enter \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} before the vertices at distance 2, and so on. Thus, the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} method visits vertices in increasing order of distance from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} and vertices that cannot be reached from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} are never visited at all. A particularly useful application of the breadth-first-search algorithm is, therefore, in computing shortest paths. To compute the shortest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to every other vertex, we use a variant of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} that uses an auxilliary array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}, of length \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}. When a new vertex \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} is added to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}, we set \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{j}]\gets \ensuremath{i}}}. In this way, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}} becomes the second last node on a shortest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}. Repeating this, by taking \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}]]}, and so on we can reconstruct the (reversal of) a shortest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}.

\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} will eventually enqueue (and eventually dequeue) every vertex
\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} such that there is a directed path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}.  Moreover,
the vertices at distance 0 from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} (\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} itself) will enter \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} before
the vertices at distance 1, which will enter \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}} before the vertices at
distance 2, and so on.  Thus, the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} method visits vertices
in increasing order of distance from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} and vertices that cannot be
reached from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} are never visited at all.
A particularly useful application of the breadth-first-search algorithm
is, therefore, in computing shortest paths.  To compute the shortest
path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to every other vertex, we use a variant of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{bfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}}
that uses an auxilliary array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}, of length \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}.  When a new vertex
\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} is added to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}, we set \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{j}]\gets \ensuremath{i}}}.  In this way, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}} becomes the
second last node on a shortest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}.  Repeating this,
by taking \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}]}]]}, and so on we can reconstruct the
(reversal of) a shortest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}.

content: The \emph{depth-first-search} \index{depth-first-search} algorithm is similar to the standard algorithm for traversing binary trees; it first fully explores one subtree before returning to the current node and then exploring the other subtree. Another way to think of depth-first-search is by saying that it is similar to breadth-first search except that it uses a stack instead of a queue. During the execution of the depth-first-search algorithm, each vertex, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, is assigned a colour, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{c}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}: \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{white}}}} if we have never seen the vertex before, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}} if we are currently visiting that vertex, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{black}}}} if we are done visiting that vertex. The easiest way to think of depth-first-search is as a recursive algorithm. It starts by visiting \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}. When visiting a vertex \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, we first mark \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} as \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}}. Next, we scan \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}'s adjacency list and recursively visit any white vertex we find in this list. Finally, we are done processing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, so we colour \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} black and return.

content: \thmlabel{dfs-graph} When given as input a Graph, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{g}}}}, that is implemented using the AdjacencyLists data structure, the \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{dfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{dfs2}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} algorithms each run in $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}+\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}})$ time.

As with the breadth-first-search algorithm, there is an underlying tree associated with each execution of depth-first-search. When a node $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}\neq \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}$ goes from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{white}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}}, this is because \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{dfs}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{i}},\ensuremath{\mathit{c}})}} was called recursively while processing some node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{i}'}. (In the case of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{dfs2}(\ensuremath{\mathit{g}},\ensuremath{\mathit{r}})}} algorithm, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is one of the nodes that replaced \ensuremath{\ensuremath{i}'} on the stack.) If we think of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{i}'} as the parent of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}, then we obtain a tree rooted at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}. In \figref{graph-dfs}, this tree is a path from vertex 0 to vertex 11. An important property of the depth-first-search algorithm is the following: Suppose that when node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is coloured \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}}, there exists a path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} to some other node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} that uses only white vertices. Then \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} will be coloured first \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}} then \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{black}}}} before \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is coloured \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{black}}}}. (This can be proven by contradiction, by considering any path $P$ from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}.) One application of this property is the detection of cycles. \index{cycle detection} Refer to \figref{dfs-cycle}. Consider some cycle, $C$, that can be reached from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}. Let \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} be the first node of $C$ that is coloured \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}}, and let \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} be the node that precedes \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} on the cycle $C$. Then, by the above property, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} will be coloured \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}} and the edge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{(\ensuremath{\mathit{j}},\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} will be considered by the algorithm while \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} is still \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{grey}}}}. Thus, the algorithm can conclude that there is a path, $P$, from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}} in the depth-first-search tree and the edge \ensuremath{\ensuremath{(\ensuremath{\mathit{j}},\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} exists. Therefore, $P$ is also a cycle.

Breadth-first search seems to have been discovered independently by Moore \cite{m59} and Lee \cite{l61} in the contexts of maze exploration and circuit routing, respectively. Adjacency-list representations of graphs were presented by Hopcroft and Tarjan \cite{ht73} as an alternative to the (then more common) adjacency-matrix representation. This representation, as well as depth-first-search, played a major part in the celebrated Hopcroft-Tarjan planarity testing algorithm \index{planarity testing} that can determine, in $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ time, if a graph can be drawn, in the plane, and in such a way that no pair of edges cross each other \cite{ht74}. In the following exercises, an undirected graph is one in which, for every \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}}, the edge $(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}},\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}})$ is present if and only if the edge $(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{j}}}},\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}})$ is present. \index{undirected graph} \index{graph!undirected}
